lesson.title: Never True: When No Number Works
lesson.summary: Learn to recognize a contradiction, an equation with no solution, where solving correctly leads to a false numerical statement instead of a value for the variable.
lesson.body:
A contradiction is a linear equation in one variable that is false for every possible value of the variable, meaning its solution set is empty. Just like an identity, solving a contradiction the normal way causes the variable terms to cancel out completely, but instead of landing on a true statement, the result is a false one, such as 4 = 9 or 0 = -7. This does not mean an error was made in the algebra; a contradiction, solved correctly, is always going to end this way, because the two sides of the original equation described two different, incompatible quantities that happened to look similar.

Solve 5x + 8 = 5x - 3. Subtract 5x from both sides: 8 = -3. This is false, since 8 does not equal negative 3, no matter what x might have been. The variable has vanished from the equation entirely, and what is left is a plain false statement, which means there is no value of x that could ever make the original equation true. Testing this conclusion with a specific number confirms it: try x = 1, giving a left side of 5(1) + 8 = 13 and a right side of 5(1) - 3 = 2, which are not equal; try x = 10, giving a left side of 58 and a right side of 47, again not equal, and this mismatch of exactly 11 will persist for every value of x, since the two sides always differ by 11.

A second example shows a contradiction hiding behind distribution rather than matching coefficients written plainly. Consider 2(x + 3) = 2x + 7. Distribute the 2 on the left: 2x + 6 = 2x + 7. Subtract 2x from both sides: 6 = 7, which is false. Just as before, the variable cancelled completely, and the false statement that remains confirms there is no value of x that makes the original equation true, even though the equation did not obviously start with matching coefficients before the 2 was distributed.

Contradictions often come from equations that represent two genuinely different rules that happen to have the same variable coefficient, so the variable terms cancel identically but the constant parts do not match. Notice that both sides here had the same coefficient of x, 5x, which is exactly why the variable disappeared; if the coefficients differed, the equation would instead reduce to a normal one-answer equation, the conditional case covered next.

This is the second of the three outcomes previewed under linear equations in one variable, and it matches the empty solution set described in that concept: no number belongs to the solution set of a contradiction, so the correct final answer is "no solution," written as the empty set, not a specific value of x and not "all real numbers."

The distinguishing test between an identity and a contradiction happens at the very last step, after the variable has already dropped out: if the remaining numerical statement is true, as in 8 = 8, the equation is an identity with infinitely many solutions; if it is false, as in 8 = -3, the equation is a contradiction with no solutions. Both outcomes are correct, meaningful results of solving, standing alongside the third and most common outcome, a conditional equation with exactly one solution, examined next.
